column5: Hochschild's introduction sets the death toll at 'eight to ten million' (from a footnote about Mark Twain) and says he took it as unproven ('statistics about mass murder are often hard to prove'); he calls it a toll of 'Holocaust dimensions'. The course's 10 million tag [ESTIMATE, CONTESTED] is right to treat it as his reading. Also: Hochschild states no African voice survives in written form for the worst years - good for the course's whose-voice theme; Morel (Liverpool shipping clerk) and G. W. Williams and William Sheppard (Black American witnesses) are the key figures

Hochschild: in the mid-1870s about 80 per cent of Africa's land area was still under indigenous rulers (course: about 10 per cent European control in 1870, mostly coastal, ESTIMATE; his figure for the mid-1870s is a rough count of the same shape). Leopold II became king 1865, studied the Spanish archives (1862) and Dutch Java forced-labour model before choosing Africa; Stanley's expedition began 1874

How the Congo claim was built (Hochschild): Leopold's International African Association (1876 conference) was a humanitarian cover; the Committee for Studies of the Upper Congo and then the International Association of the Congo were fronts he alone funded; Stanley worked for him from 1879; treaties with chiefs were collected 'as soon as possible'; a subordinate wrote there was no question of granting political power to Africans. Supports the course's 'treaty proves a signature not consent' and adds the cover-organisation chain; the Congo basin had 200+ ethnic groups with fragmented opposition

Treaty evidence for the course's 'treaty proves a signature not consent' example: Stanley claimed treaties with over 450 chiefs; Leopold ordered them brief but granting 'everything'; a sample treaty of 01/04/1884 (Ngombi and Mafela) gave sovereignty, tolls and rights to labour 'by labour or otherwise' for a piece of cloth a month; chiefs could not read the language. Use as the worked-example evidence in lesson 2 (replace or add to the generic Chief X example). The Congo's borders would stretch from Zurich to Moscow on a map of Europe

Berlin Conference (15/11/1884 to Feb 1885): Hochschild says, contrary to myth, it did not partition Africa; it set free-trade and navigation ground rules and settled disputes at the Congo mouth, while partition followed through many later bilateral treaties. Leopold lobbied through proxies (Sanford, Stanley as US adviser, Bleichroder); the US recognised his association first on 22/04/1884; no African present. Check the course's Berlin wording does not say the conference 'carved up' Africa; Free State named 29/05/1885, about 76 times the size of Belgium

Tools of conquest in the Congo: breech-loading and repeating rifles, Maxim gun, quinine/medical advance, steamboats ('house that walks on water'); 430 whites in the Congo by end of 1889, under half Belgian, mostly officers on leave; a few thousand whites ruling about twenty million Africans (Hochschild's estimate). Anti-Slavery Conference Brussels from 11/1889 let Leopold levy import duties, undercutting Berlin free trade; Belgian Parliament interest-free 25M franc loan in 1890 in exchange for will bequeathing the Congo to Belgium. Supports Module 1 lesson on 'tools of empire' and humanitarian cover for conquest

Emin Pasha Relief Expedition 1887-90 (Stanley): brutality and heavy losses, over half of 389 in the vanguard died. Context for explorer-as-agent-of-conquest; not needed in course beyond an optional line

George Washington Williams (African American veteran, historian, minister), Open Letter to Leopold written at Stanley Falls 18/07/1890 after six months in the Congo: first systematic human-rights indictment of the Free State. Charges: treaties obtained by trickery and gin (so land claims invalid), Stanley a tyrant, riverside posts seizing food at gunpoint and burning villages, brutal chain gangs. Primary-voice evidence for Module 1 Congo lesson; shows contemporary protest 14 years before Morel. Caveat: Hochschild notes Williams embellished his own record (not a colonel, claimed a doctorate)

Williams used the phrase 'crimes against humanity' in a letter to the US Secretary of State (1890); died 02/08/1891 aged 41 at Blackpool; Leopold's side attacked his credibility ('so-called colonel'), yet Hochschild says virtually everything he wrote was later corroborated. Good source-criticism example: a flawed messenger with accurate content. Also: close to a thousand Europeans and Americans had visited by 1890 and only Williams spoke out

Mechanics of the Free State: 'vacant land' decree 1885 made state owner of all unclaimed land and its produce; concession companies with state holding ~50 per cent; ivory commissions on a sliding scale (6 to 10 per cent) 1890 incentivised forcing low prices; brass-rod currency, no money transactions for Africans; porter conscription (e.g. 300 porters in 1891 none returned); chicotte hippo-hide whip (100+ lashes often fatal); Force Publique formed 1888, over 19,000 men by about 1900, over half the state budget by late 1890s, posts 183 in 1900 to 313 in 1908; more than a dozen ethnic groups rebelled (Yaka to 1906, Chokwe 20 years); Tshamakele cave, 178 bodies. Use for Module 1 lesson 3 (Congo): mechanism of extraction, and for the argument that violence was organised by incentives, not just individual cruelty. Hochschild also stresses Africans as intermediaries/foremen and that pre-colonial Congo had its own wars

African resistance to the Free State: Nzansu's rising (killed Rommel 05/12/1893, fought on to about 1899); Luluabourg mutiny 1895 (Kandolo; rebels held Kasai for over half a year, Yamba-Yamba and Kimpuki killed 1908); the Batetela-linked northeast mutiny 1897 of 3,000 soldiers lasting three years (rebels aimed at an independent state). Hochschild calls them precursors of later anticolonial guerrilla wars. Add to Module 1/2 as African agency alongside Maji Maji and Herero and Nama. Also: forced recruitment ('volunteers' in chains, about three quarters died before delivery per a 1892 official) and Tippu Tip appointed governor of eastern province 1887 (collaboration with Afro-Arab slavers; Leopold's antislavery campaign was selective). Ilanga's testimony (recorded by Canisius) is a rare African voice, a good primary-source quote for the lesson

Children's colonies: Leopold's 27/04/1890 order for state colonies to supply soldiers; Catholic missions took 'orphans' (often made orphans by Force Publique raids), death rates often over 50 per cent. Also white mortality: before 1895 about a third of Free State white agents died there; recruits were adventurers drawn by ivory commissions (Leon Rom as example). Context for the incentive structure; optional detail

Conrad (Korzeniowski) spent about six months in the Congo in 1890 (steamer trip Stanley Pool to Stanley Falls); Heart of Darkness (written 1898-99) draws on what he saw (dead porters on the caravan route, chained labour). Hochschild argues Leon Rom (head decoration at Stanley Falls 1895, per Century Magazine) is a likely model for Kurtz, but this is his inference ('we will never know'). Achebe's critique of the novel's portrayal of Africans. Optional literary-sources aside in Module 1; flag the Rom link as Hochschild's hypothesis, not established fact

William Sheppard (African American Presbyterian missionary, Congo from 05/1890): reached the Kuba capital 1892, first outsider to document Kuba court (sophisticated political system, royal police, archive of art); Kuba kingdom stayed outside the state until Leopold's forces looted the capital about 1900. Counter-image to 'blank map' Africa, and a Module 3 diaspora link (African American agency; Sen. Morgan's back-to-Africa motive). Rubber boom: Dunlop pneumatic tyre 1888-90 triggered demand; wild rubber vines covered nearly half the Congo. Causal link for lesson 3: rubber price rise through the 1890s -> forced labour quotas

Rubber system (core of Module 1 Congo lesson): quotas (ABIR: 3-4 kg dried rubber per adult male per fortnight; Mongala basin ~24 days a month in forest), hostage-taking of women/children (instructions in the state's Manuel du Voyageur et du Resident au Congo), numbered metal disks, company militias ('sentries'), commissions (one agent in 1903 earned eight times his salary). Economics: ABIR cost 1.35 francs/kg vs sale up to 10 francs/kg (profit over 700 per cent); Congo rubber earnings rose ninety-six times 1890-1904; most profitable colony in Africa by 1900; Leopold's wild-rubber boom lasted about two decades until plantation rubber matured. Check the course's rubber figures against these

Severed hands: Sheppard in 1899 counted 81 smoked right hands at a chief's camp; hands used as proof cartridges had been used on people (not wasted on game); official Charles Lemaire later wrote that gathering rubber required cutting off hands, noses and ears (Hochschild quotes). Leon Fievez quoted justifying killing 100 to supply food. Vandervelde later called Leopold's arches the 'Arches of the Severed Hands'. Use in lesson 3 with a caution that hand-cutting was a system of proof/discipline run by soldiers and allies; Hochschild treats it as deliberate policy by admission of senior officials

Matadi-Stanley Pool railway (built 1890-98, 241 miles): official toll 132 whites and 1,800 non-whites, with some estimates of about 1,800 a year in the first two years; 540 Chinese brought in 1892, about 300 died or fled; workers from West Africa, Barbados, Hong Kong. Over 11 million pounds of rubber a year by 1900. Infrastructure built to extract, not develop. Also: Leopold kept profits secret, issued 100M+ francs of bonds, spent on Belgian monuments; Commission for the Protection of the Natives 1896 was a PR device (met twice, no power); Charles Stokes hanged 1895 caused first real European outcry because victim was white; missionaries as witnesses (Sjoblom 1896-97 on hands paid with brass rods; Fox Bourne, Aborigines Protection Society); Tervuren exhibition 1897 with 267 Congolese displayed (human zoo); Leopold never visited the Congo

E. D. Morel's deduction (shipping clerk, Elder Dempster, late 1890s): ship records vs the Free State's published trade figures showed ~80 per cent of imports were non-trade goods (arms, ammunition), and exports to Europe worth about five times goods shipped for Africans, so Africans were not being paid: forced labour. A source-method example (cross-checking two sets of records) good for the Module 1 Congo lesson and the 'how do we know' skill

Morel campaign: left Elder Dempster 1901 aged 28, founded West African Mail 1903 (funded by Liverpool Quaker businessmen e.g. John Holt); Hochschild says his facts and figures hold up and many later statistics trace to him. Morel's distinctive thesis: the atrocities followed necessarily from the system (state owning all land and produce), not from bad individuals; printed ABIR hostage-detention form (1903) and Force Publique recruitment bounty order (90 francs per man, 65 per youth, 15 per boy); missionary photographs of mutilated children; Canisius testimony (900+ Budja killed in a six-week campaign for 20 tons a month of rubber). House of Commons resolution May 1903. Note Morel's own limits: free-trade faith and British Congo-reform vs. later views of empire

Casement Report (British consul Roger Casement, 3.5 months in interior 1903, report published early 1904): official, sober, with depositions; the Foreign Office stripped witness names under pressure from the Brussels minister Phipps and Elder Dempster's Jones, which weakened it against Leopold's reply. Diary entries record depopulation (e.g. 93 people left in a village once of many hundreds) and hostage-holding. Casement's own verdict: the system itself was wrong, not just excesses. First official government evidence after Morel's private-source campaign; use as a primary-source anchor. Casement's later fate (1916 execution, diaries) is a separate story; mention only if the course already does

Congo Reform Association founded by Morel with Casement's funding; first public meeting 23/03/1904 at Liverpool's Philharmonic Hall (1,000+ attended). Often called the first modern human-rights campaign. Hochschild's own caveat: the leaders were white Britons acting for Africans whose names went unrecorded

Congo reform movement as Hochschild frames it: mass campaign (60+ mass meetings by end of 1905, slide shows with photos by Alice Seeley Harris, 'Congo Sundays'), but with limits: Morel saw the Congo as a unique evil and not a fault of colonialism itself, defended British rule in Nigeria, idealised pre-colonial Africa, and ignored forced labour in British colonies. Tension between humanitarian reform and a structural critique. Good prompt for Module 1 critical-thinking question: why was reform support wide only because it did not threaten other empires? Also state surveillance of missionaries (governor-general's spy instructions)

African participants in the reform campaign: Hezekiah Andrew Shanu (Nigerian-born clerk and businessman in Boma) secretly sent Morel the secret Caudron trial papers (agent Charles Caudron accused of murdering at least 122 Africans; sentence cut for 'extenuating circumstances'); exposed 1905, boycotted, died by suicide July 1905. Shows Africans inside the Free State as informants and the state's use of show trials. Also: Leopold's mistress scandal (Caroline, 16, when he was 65) cost him Belgian public support; Belgians resented profits going to monuments and Riviera estates. Optional colour

DEATH TOLL (key for the course's ESTIMATE/CONTESTED table): Hochschild's chain of reasoning: no census until 1924 (population then reckoned at about 10 million); 1919 Belgian government commission said population 'reduced by half' since Stanley; Liebrechts (top Free State official) said the same in 1920; Jan Vansina (ethnographer) judged 'at least a half' loss 1880-1920 from local sources (priests, oral tradition, genealogies); Hochschild concludes about 10 million. Casement estimated 60 per cent loss in one rubber district. Local headcounts (Vangroenweghe) show far more women than men (e.g. Inongo 1907: 402 adult women, 275 men). Method caveat: percentage is more reliable than absolute number; estimate rests on a 1924 base and the 'half' premise, spans 1880-1920 and includes the post-1908 period. Course should keep it [ESTIMATE]/[CONTESTED], quote the 'about half' evidence, and name the four causes (killing, starvation/exhaustion, disease, falling births)

Hochschild states plainly the killing was 'of genocidal proportions' but 'not, strictly speaking, a genocide' (aim was labour, not elimination of a group); outright murder was not the major cause, disease and famine plus birth-rate collapse were; sleeping sickness (500,000 deaths estimated in 1901 alone) and smallpox are the factors Leopold's apologists cite, which Hochschild argues were worsened by malnutrition and trauma. Specific documented incidents: 1,308 hands to Fievez in a day (Koelnische Zeitung 1896); Simon Roi reported 6,000 cartridges in six months on the Momboyo; Budja campaign over 1,300 killed; ABIR post sent 159 firearms and 40,355 rounds in 1903. Use these as sourced examples, not as totals. Also 30,000 refugees into French territory by 1900

Leopold's counter-propaganda (source-criticism material): Press Bureau set up 09/1904 behind front groups; secret payments to editors across Europe (Times and Koelnische Zeitung Brussels correspondents by 1907); paid or hosted visitors (Mountmorres, Mary French Sheldon, 'Truth about the Congo' magazine in Wagons-Lits sleeping cars); 'whataboutism' publications on abuses in British territories; a bagman's letter records the instruction 'Journalists and writers won't give you receipts'. Lesson: official reassurance and favourable travel accounts can be bought or staged (hostages released and prison demolished before a VIP visit). US: American Congo Reform Association 1904 with Mark Twain (King Leopold's Soliloquy 1905) and Booker T. Washington; Leopold offered concession shares to Aldrich, Guggenheim, Rockefeller Jr., Ryan, which blunted US action; Sen. John Tyler Morgan wanted ten million Black Americans 'planted' in the Congo (link to Module 3 Garvey/back-to-Africa debate)

Commission of Inquiry 1904-05 (three judges, 370 depositions): intended as a whitewash but its 150-page report confirmed most of Casement's and Morel's charges; published 11/1905 after Leopold released a fake 'summary' via a phantom 'West African Missionary Association' a day earlier to mislead the press. Chief Lontulu laid 110 twigs for his dead. Kowalsky scandal (Hearst's New York American, 10/12/1906) exposed Leopold's US lobbying bribes and shifted US policy. Teaches how an official inquiry and its spin were separated: read the report, not the press summary

Commission of Inquiry African testimony (370 depositions) was never published; sealed in Brussels until the 1980s. Annexation by Belgium 03/1908 (formal handover 15/11/1908): Belgium assumed 110M francs of debts, 45.5M for Leopold's building projects and a further 50M francs 'as gratitude' (to be extracted from the Congo itself): Leopold sold, not gave. Reform movement's own 'Belgian solution' reflected that few in 1900s imagined independence; Williams's 1890 call for rule 'local, not European' was not echoed for decades. Course Module 1 should say the 1908 handover ended the personal regime but Hochschild stresses continuity of forced labour in the Kasai rubber area after 1908

Sheppard libel trial (Leopoldville, 1909; Vandervelde defended): rubber terror continued under Compagnie du Kasai after the 1908 handover; Kuba revolt about 1908 (about 180 killed; elders' fetish said to turn bullets into water, a motif the course can link to Maji Maji's maji); British vice consul Thesiger's Kasai report 1908. Leopold died 17/12/1909 aged 74. Casement later investigated Putumayo rubber atrocities in Peru (1910-11) and linked colonial exploitation of Congo and Ireland. Gives a Module 2 link: bullet-turning-water belief appears in Kuba revolt as well as Maji Maji

Aftermath: Morel called the 1908 Belgian takeover only 'a partial victory'. System continuity (same personnel, Force Publique unchanged, 'taxes in kind' increased, ABIR shareholder on the budget committee). Reforms phased over three years from 1909-10; atrocity reports fell to a trickle; Harrises reported 'immense improvement' 1912; British recognition of the Belgian Congo 1913; CRA wound up 16/06/1913. Morel's main unmet aim: African ownership of land. Foreign Office reply shows British colonies did not treat land as African-owned either. Also note Morel's early 1909 warning about South Africa's all-white Union (links Module 5 and 1910). Use for lesson on 'end of Free State, not end of forced labour'

Did reform work? Hochschild's answer is sobering: atrocity reports fell after 1908 mainly because of shift to cultivated rubber and to head taxes as the compulsion, not because the reform campaign dismantled forced labour (forced labour continued into WWI, mining, 1921-31 railway rebuild and WWII: legal maximum 120 days per man per year; Moto mines 26,579 lashes in first half of 1920). Leopold's personal profit: Marchal's 'conservative' 220 million francs (about .1bn today). Good nuance for Module 1: Belgian takeover = change of form, not end of coercion. Jules Marchal is the leading specialist historian cited here

'Why the Congo?': Hochschild argues Congo was not uniquely murderous within equatorial rubber Africa: French Congo concession system had equal brutality and roughly 50 per cent population loss in rubber areas (20,000 forced labourers died on 1920s railway), German Cameroons imitated Leopold; Herero genocide 1904-06 (von Trotha's extermination order; about 80,000 Herero in 1903, under 20,000 in 1906) got little protest including from Morel's circle. Reform movement focused on a 'safe target' (no British/American complicity, small Belgium). Links directly to Module 2 Herero and Nama; add cross-reference. Conrad: 'All Europe contributed to the making of Kurtz'. Also US war in the Philippines mentioned for comparison

Biographical aftermath of the reformers: Casement hanged 03/08/1916 after the Easter Rising gun-running attempt; British circulated his diaries to discredit him; his 1916 trial speech on self-government influenced Nehru. Morel opposed WWI, jailed 1917, MP 1922-24, died 12/11/1924. Not needed in Module 1 beyond optional one-line; Casement's anticolonial speech is a possible Module 3/4 link

The 'great forgetting': Free State archives burned for eight days in 08/1908 (Leopold: 'they have no right to know what I did there'); the Commission of Inquiry testimony stayed sealed in the Belgian Foreign Ministry until Jules Marchal won access (decades later); Belgian textbooks and the Tervuren museum omit the deaths; 1914 'brave little Belgium' propaganda about severed hands (false) overwrote memory of Leopold's real ones. Direct source-criticism lesson for Module 1: why the death toll is an estimate (records destroyed, no census until 1924). Cite as evidence for the [ESTIMATE] label; note that Hochschild says the Royal Museum for Central Africa had no mention of the toll when he wrote (it has since been renovated and reopened in 2018 with changes, so [check current])

Congo at independence (1960) per Hochschild: fewer than thirty African university graduates, no Congolese army officers, engineers, agronomists or physicians, and only 3 of about 5,000 management-level civil-service posts held by Africans; mass demonstrations in Leopoldville 1959 suppressed by the Force Publique. Belongs to Module 4 (independence) and Module 7 (Congo wars): cross-reference. The 'Leopold as Bishop de Hemptinne' legend is colour only

Lumumba and Mobutu per Hochschild: independence 30/06/1960; Lumumba prime minister after the first national election; Hochschild says a US NSC subcommittee including Allen Dulles authorised his assassination (Bissell/Eisenhower quotes), poison supplied to the CIA station, but he was killed in January 1961 in Katanga by Congolese opponents with Belgian officers and a Belgian pilot involved. Mobutu: coup 1965, ruled 32 years, renamed country Zaire 1971, personal wealth peak est. bn, US aid over bn. Hochschild's parallel Leopold-Mobutu (one-man rule, wealth from land) is his interpretation. Check against the course's Module 4/6/7 Congo wording; US role in the plot vs. the killing itself is where specialists differ (Belgian parliamentary inquiry 2001 found Belgian moral responsibility)

Afterword (2005 ed.) on the toll: Hochschild says no change needed to ch.15; 'without accurate census data... a matter of estimates', but knowledgeable estimates are high; adds Isidore Ndaywel e Nziem (Congolese historian, Histoire generale du Congo, 1998) at roughly thirteen million, higher than his own. So the specialist range runs from lower figures (contested by Belgian defenders and some academics) to about 13 million. Add Ndaywel as a named higher estimate in the course's death-toll table and keep the 8 to 10 million as the mainstream-popular figure; also say the 1919 commission and Vansina give 'about half' not an absolute number. Hochschild does not name low-end specialists here (course should look elsewhere if it wants them: e.g. Stengers/Vellut critique is only alluded to as 'conservative Africa scholar' in the Guardian)

Reception: Belgian 'old colonial' groups attacked the book as sensationalist; Belgian historian Jean Stengers (conservative) predicted it would be forgotten; Belgian government's 2001 parliamentary inquiry confirmed Ludo De Witte's findings on Belgian complicity in Lumumba's death and issued an apology (the US has not). The 2005 Tervuren exhibition 'Memory of the Congo' still omitted hostages and the forced-labour system. Hochschild's own limits: Africans appear as full actors too little; the key African voices are the Boelaert/Hulstaert 1950s interviews (Centre Aequatoria). Kevin Grant, A Civilised Savagery (2005), adds that Baptist lantern shows pre-dated the CRA and that Morel glossed over Portuguese cocoa forced labour (linked to Cadbury)

Hochschild's closing thesis: colonialism is not the only cause of Africa's troubles; he points to the position of women, hero-worship of strongmen, and a long history of indigenous slavery 'woven into the social fabric' (a contested, popular-history claim, not mainstream consensus among Africanists). Congo wars: he gives a vague 'a million or more' deaths (early 2000s figure; IRC surveys later gave about 5.4M excess deaths 1998-2007, contested [check current]). Present as Hochschild's interpretation, to sit beside the course's Module 6/7 treatments; do not adopt the strongmen/indigenous-slavery causal claims as course fact

Notes section correction to the afterword: Ndaywel e Nziem's 13 million (1998 first ed.) was later LOWERED by him to ten million (personal communication, per Hochschild's note), which 'would still imply a 50 per cent loss'. So the named higher estimate is ~10M, not 13M; use '13 million (1998 ed., later revised to 10 million)'. Notes also name the sources behind the toll: 1919 commission via Guebels 1954; Vansina's intro to Vangroenweghe; 1924 census via the 1924 colonial-congress report; sleeping sickness defence illustrated by Stengers. Marchal's profit estimate (220M francs, ~$1.1bn) is a sum of 110M in loans spent in Europe plus ~110M off-the-books rubber profits 1898-1908; excludes earlier rubber and smaller firms. Lumumba plot authorisation cited to the Church Committee (20/11/1975) via Kelly

Note on pan-Africanism (ch.17 note): even the Second Pan-African Congress in Paris (1919, Du Bois) did not demand full independence for African colonies; Hochschild uses this to say demands for African self-government were almost unspoken until the 1920s-30s. Cross-check with the course's Module 3 lesson on the Congresses (Welsh/Garvey reading may say otherwise for 1919 resolutions)

Bibliography gives the specialist literature behind the Congo claims, useful for the course's further-reading and for the 'where specialists disagree' line: Jules Marchal (4 vols, best overall), Daniel Vangroenweghe, Jan Vansina, Robert Harms (argues the end of 'red rubber' reassessed, 1975), Jean Stengers (conservative Belgian historian who emphasises the sleeping-sickness argument), Roger Anstey, Catherine Coquery-Vidrovitch (French Congo), S.J.S. Cookey, Ruth Slade, David Lagergren, David Northrup (Eastern Congo labour), Jean-Luc Vellut (compiles the bibliography; Hochschild cites Vellut and Vansina for pre-colonial violence like hand-cutting of dead enemies). Hochschild also warns his Stanley biography sources (Bierman, McLynn) are contested by Tim Jeal (2007), who defends Stanley and argues the treaties were less onerous and that Leopold doctored them; the original treaties mostly vanished. This is a genuine dispute behind the course's 'treaty' example
